title: Physics II: Waves, Electricity and Magnetism, and Heat
description: Waves and light, electric and magnetic fields, induction, and heat and the limits on engines, with calculations that connect each idea to something you can measure.
audience: A capable adult who has finished Discere's mechanics course (forces, energy, momentum) and is comfortable with algebra and powers. Sines appear in the light lessons; a short recap is built in.
outcomes: You'll be able to find the period of an oscillator and the speed, wavelength and frequency of a wave.
You'll be able to predict standing waves, beats, fringes and Doppler shifts.
You'll be able to trace a ray through glass and locate an image.
You'll be able to compute the force between charges, the field and voltage between plates, and forces on moving charges.
You'll be able to apply induction and transformers.
You'll be able to calculate heat, conduction and radiation, and use the ideal gas law and first law.
You'll be able to state the efficiency limit of an engine and explain why entropy rises.

sources.title: OpenStax, University Physics Volume 2 (thermodynamics, electricity and magnetism, optics)
NIST, The International System of Units (SI) and the 2019 redefinition
PhET Interactive Simulations (University of Colorado Boulder): Wave on a String, Charges and Fields, Faraday's Law, Gas Properties

modules.title: Oscillations, waves and light
modules.summary: Things that repeat, how repeats travel as waves, and how light bends and forms images.

modules.summary: Charge, fields, voltage, magnetic force, induction and the electromagnetic wave.

modules.title: Heat and thermodynamics
modules.summary: Temperature, heat, how energy moves, gases and the limit on engines.

lessons.title: Things that repeat
lessons.objective: Find the period and frequency of a mass on a spring and a pendulum.

concepts.title: Period and frequency
concepts.summary: The period T is the time for one cycle and the frequency f = 1/T is cycles per second (hertz).

concepts.title: Simple harmonic motion
concepts.summary: Motion under a restoring force proportional to displacement; a mass on a spring has T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k) and a small-angle pendulum has T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

misconceptions: A heavier mass swings a pendulum more slowly. The mass cancels; only length and g set the period.
A larger swing takes longer. For small swings the period does not depend on the amplitude.
Period and frequency are the same number. They are reciprocals.
sequence: Watch a mass bounce: displacement against time is a repeating curve.
Name amplitude, period and frequency.
Restoring force proportional to displacement gives the spring formula.
Pendulum: gravity supplies the restoring force; mass cancels.
Energy swaps between motion and storage each cycle (link to the earlier energy lessons).
examples: L = 1 m, g = 9.8 m/s2: T = 2.01 s. Quadrupling L doubles T.

figures.shows: Displacement against time for a spring, with sliders for mass, stiffness and amplitude (cases fixed in the lesson).
figures.learnerAction: Switch cases and read the period off the graph.

figures.shows: Pendulum with swing and energy bars at three positions.

questionPlan.sample: A 0.5 kg mass is on a spring with k = 200 N/m. What is its period in seconds, to three decimals?
A pendulum has period 2 s. A second pendulum is four times as long. What is its period in seconds?
A pendulum swings with period 0.25 s. What is its frequency in Hz?

lessons.title: A wave is a travelling pattern
lessons.objective: Use v = f x wavelength and tell transverse from longitudinal waves.

concepts.title: Wave speed
concepts.summary: v = f x wavelength: speed equals frequency times the length of one cycle in space.

concepts.title: Transverse and longitudinal
concepts.summary: The medium moves across the direction of travel in transverse waves and along it in longitudinal waves; the wave carries energy, not matter.

misconceptions: The water travels with the wave. The pattern moves; each bit of the medium only oscillates around where it started.
A higher frequency wave travels faster. In a given medium the speed is fixed by the medium; higher frequency means shorter wavelength.
Sound is transverse. In air sound is a longitudinal pressure wave.
sequence: Wiggle one end of a rope. The pulse travels; a marked bead only goes up and down.
Define wavelength, frequency and speed; derive v = f lambda from one cycle passing per period.
Sound in air, 343 m/s at 20 degrees C; light, about 3.00e8 m/s.
Transverse versus longitudinal.
What changes when a wave enters a new medium: speed and wavelength change, frequency does not.
examples: Sound at 440 Hz in air at 343 m/s: wavelength = 343 / 440 = 0.78 m.
A 100 MHz radio wave: wavelength = 3.00e8 / 1.00e8 = 3.0 m.

figures.shows: Snapshot of a wave in space and a time record at one point, with wavelength and period marked.
figures.learnerAction: Toggle between snapshot and time record.

figures.shows: Spring-coil compressions versus rope wiggles, with a tracer on one coil or bead.

questionPlan.sample: Sound travels at 343 m/s. What is the wavelength of a 440 Hz note, in metres to two decimals?
A radio station broadcasts at 100 MHz. Radio waves travel at 3.00e8 m/s. What is the wavelength in metres?
In a sound wave in air, the air molecules move
questionPlan.answer: Back and forth along the direction of travel
choices: Up and down across the direction of travel
Back and forth along the direction of travel
Along with the wave to the listener

lessons.title: When waves add
lessons.objective: Predict standing waves, beats and double-slit fringes from superposition.

concepts.title: Superposition
concepts.summary: Where waves overlap, their displacements add; peaks meeting peaks reinforce and peaks meeting troughs cancel.

concepts.title: Standing wave
concepts.summary: A string fixed at both ends supports waves with f_n = n v / (2L), where n = 1, 2, 3.

misconceptions: Waves bounce off each other like balls. They pass through each other and add while overlapping.
Beats are a separate third wave. They are the changing loudness from two close frequencies.
Fringes show light is a stream of tiny balls. Double-slit fringes need waves; the pattern is the sum of two.
sequence: Add two pulses on a rope: constructive and destructive.
A wave reflected at the fixed ends: only some frequencies fit, n half wavelengths in length L.
Beat frequency |f1 - f2|, as in tuning a guitar.
Double slit: fringe spacing = wavelength x L / d.
Why a musical note has harmonics.
examples: String L = 0.5 m, wave speed 200 m/s: f1 = 200/(2 x 0.5) = 200 Hz, f3 = 600 Hz.
Light 500 nm, slits 0.10 mm apart, screen 2 m away: spacing = 500e-9 x 2 / 1.0e-4 = 0.010 m = 1.0 cm.

figures.shows: Two sine waves and their sum, with phase sliders as fixed cases (in phase, half-cycle apart, slightly different frequency).
figures.learnerAction: Switch cases and watch the sum.

figures.shows: String modes n = 1 to 4 with nodes marked.

questionPlan.sample: A string of length 0.5 m carries waves at 200 m/s. What is the frequency of the third harmonic, in Hz?
Two tuning forks sound at 440 Hz and 444 Hz. How many beats per second are heard?
Light of 500 nm passes two slits 0.10 mm apart onto a screen 2.0 m away. What is the spacing between bright fringes, in cm?

lessons.title: Loudness, pitch and moving sources
lessons.objective: Use the decibel scale and the Doppler shift.

concepts.title: Decibel level
concepts.summary: Level = 10 log10(I / I0) with I0 = 1e-12 W/m2; every factor of 10 in intensity adds 10 dB.

concepts.title: Doppler shift
concepts.summary: For a source approaching a still listener, f' = f v / (v - v_source).

misconceptions: Twice the dB is twice the loudness. A 3 dB step doubles intensity; 10 dB is ten times the intensity.
A siren changes pitch as it passes because it vibrates differently. The source's frequency is constant; the waves bunch up in front and spread out behind.
A moving observer and a moving source give the same shift. The two formulas differ.
sequence: Why logarithms: hearing spans a trillion-fold intensity range.
Decibel arithmetic.
Doppler: a source running through its own waves compresses the wavelength in front.
Apply with numbers and give the sign convention.
Applications: radar speed guns, redshift, medical ultrasound.
examples: 500 Hz source approaching at 34.3 m/s, v = 343 m/s: f' = 500 x 343 / (343 - 34.3) = 555.6 Hz.

figures.shows: dB against intensity on a log axis.
Wave fronts from a moving source: tight ahead, spread behind.
figures.learnerAction: Move the source speed between fixed cases.

questionPlan.sample: A sound has intensity 1e-6 W/m2. With I0 = 1e-12 W/m2 what is its level in dB?
One machine gives 70 dB. Ten identical machines run together. What is the total level in dB?
A 500 Hz siren approaches at 34.3 m/s. Sound speed is 343 m/s. What frequency is heard, in Hz to the nearest Hz?

lessons.title: Why light bends
lessons.objective: Apply the law of refraction and find a critical angle.

concepts.title: Refraction
concepts.summary: Light changes speed between media, v = c/n, and bends so that n1 sin(theta1) = n2 sin(theta2).

concepts.title: Total internal reflection
concepts.summary: From a denser to a less dense medium, beyond the critical angle theta_c = arcsin(n2/n1) all the light reflects.

misconceptions: Light bends toward the surface on entering glass. It bends toward the normal, the line at right angles to the surface.
Angles are measured from the surface. They are measured from the normal.
Refraction needs a bent beam. Light at 0 degrees to the normal goes straight in, and slows.
sequence: A recap of sine as a ratio in a right triangle, with a calculator.
Marching soldiers hitting mud at an angle: why a wavefront turns when speed changes.
Snell's law and the normal.
Going out: critical angle and total internal reflection (fibre optics, prisms).
Dispersion: n depends on wavelength, so white light spreads.
examples: Air (n = 1.00) to glass (n = 1.50) at 30 degrees: sin(theta2) = 0.5/1.5 = 0.333, theta2 = 19.5 degrees.
Glass to air: critical angle = arcsin(1/1.5) = 41.8 degrees.

figures.shows: Ray hitting an interface with a normal, angles marked, switchable between air-glass, glass-air and glass-air beyond critical.
figures.learnerAction: Choose a case and read the angles.

What is the critical angle for light going from glass (n = 1.50) to air (n = 1.00), in degrees to one decimal?
On entering glass from air at an angle, a ray bends

lessons.title: Lenses and images
lessons.objective: Locate an image with the thin-lens equation and describe it.

concepts.title: Thin-lens equation
concepts.summary: 1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i, with magnification m = -d_i / d_o.

concepts.title: Real and virtual images
concepts.summary: A real image forms where rays meet and can be caught on a screen; a virtual image is where rays appear to come from.

misconceptions: Images sit on the lens. They form at a distance set by f and the object distance.
A negative magnification means a smaller image. It means inverted; the size is the absolute value.
A virtual image does not exist. It is seen by the eye but cannot be caught on a screen.
sequence: Three rays from an object tip through a converging lens.
Where they meet is the image: the equation does the same job.
Sign conventions and what negative values mean.
Cases: beyond 2f, between f and 2f, inside f (magnifying glass).
The eye and a camera as a lens and a screen.
examples: f = 10 cm, object 30 cm away: 1/d_i = 1/10 - 1/30 = 1/15, d_i = 15 cm, m = -15/30 = -0.5 (real, inverted, half size).
Object 5 cm from the same lens: 1/d_i = 1/10 - 1/5 = -1/10, d_i = -10 cm, m = +2 (virtual, upright, twice size).

figures.shows: Principal-axis diagram with object, lens, three rays, and image; switchable object distances.

lessons.title: Charge and the force between charges
lessons.objective: Calculate the force between point charges with Coulomb's law.

concepts.title: Electric charge
concepts.summary: A conserved property that comes in two signs; like charges repel and unlike attract.

concepts.title: Coulomb's law
concepts.summary: F = k q1 q2 / r^2 with k = 8.99e9 N m2/C2.

misconceptions: Charge is created by rubbing. It is moved, not made; the total is conserved.
Doubling the distance halves the force. The force falls with the square, to a quarter.
A charged object only attracts other charges. It also attracts neutral objects by polarising them.
sequence: Rubbed balloon and paper: charge moves.
The two signs and the rule for attraction.
Coulomb's law, with units and the size of a coulomb (1 uC is a realistic lab charge).
Inverse-square: link to gravity from the earlier course.
Compare the electric force to gravity between two protons.
examples: Doubling to 0.20 m: F = 0.225 N.

figures.shows: Force against separation, an inverse-square curve.
Two charges with force arrows, switchable like or unlike.

questionPlan.sample: Two 2.0 uC charges are 0.30 m apart. Use k = 8.99e9. What is the force in newtons to two decimals?
The distance between two charges triples. By what factor does the force change? Give the factor as a decimal to three places.
A positive and a negative charge are brought close. The force is
choices: Perpendicular to the line joining them

lessons.title: Fields and voltage
lessons.objective: Use field and potential difference to find forces and speeds of charges.

concepts.title: Electric field
concepts.summary: E = F / q: the force per unit charge; between parallel plates E = V / d.

concepts.title: Potential difference
concepts.summary: The energy per unit charge: a charge q moved through V gains qV of energy.

misconceptions: Voltage is a quantity that flows. It is a difference in energy per charge; charge flows.
Field lines are paths charges follow. They show the force direction at each point.
A stronger field always means a higher voltage. Voltage is field integrated over distance.
sequence: Define the field by a test charge.
Parallel plates: uniform field and E = V / d.
Energy gained by a charge crossing a potential difference; electron-volt.
Speed of an electron accelerated through 100 V.
Link to the circuits course: a battery maintains a potential difference.
examples: 12 V across plates 0.020 m apart: E = 600 V/m.
An electron through 100 V gains 100 eV = 1.60e-17 J. Setting 1/2 m v^2 equal: v = sqrt(2 x 1.602e-17 / 9.109e-31) = 5.9e6 m/s.

figures.shows: Parallel plates with uniform field arrows and equipotential lines, plus point-charge field lines; switchable.

questionPlan.sample: The plates are 0.020 m apart and have 12 V across them. What is the field between them in V/m?
An electron is accelerated through 250 V. How many electron-volts of energy does it gain?
A charge of 2.0 C passes through a potential difference of 1.5 V. How many joules of energy does it gain?

lessons.title: Magnetic force
lessons.objective: Find the magnetic force on moving charges and currents, and the radius of a circular path.

concepts.title: Force on a moving charge
concepts.summary: F = q v B sin(theta), perpendicular to both v and B, so it changes direction but not speed.

concepts.title: Force on a wire
concepts.summary: F = B I L sin(theta) for a straight wire of length L carrying current I.

misconceptions: Magnets push on any charge. Only moving charges feel a magnetic force, and only the component of velocity across the field.
The force is along the field. It is at right angles to both v and B.
Magnetic forces speed up the particle. They do no work and only turn it.
sequence: Compass and bar-magnet field lines; the Earth as a magnet.
A moving charge in a field: the right-hand rule.
Circular motion: the force supplies the centripetal force, r = m v / (q B).
A current is moving charge: force on a wire, how a motor works.
Applications: mass spectrometer, cyclotron, speakers.
examples: Wire 0.25 m long carrying 4 A across a 0.50 T field: F = 0.5 x 4 x 0.25 = 0.50 N.

figures.shows: Charged particle spiralling in a field into the page, with velocity, B and force vectors.
figures.learnerAction: Switch between positive and negative charge and speeds.

questionPlan.sample: A wire 0.25 m long carries 4.0 A across a 0.50 T field at right angles. What is the force in newtons?
A particle moves at right angles to a field. If its speed doubles and everything else is the same, by what factor does the orbit radius change?
What does a magnetic field do to the speed of a charged particle moving through it?
questionPlan.answer: Nothing; it changes only the direction
choices: Nothing; it changes only the direction

lessons.title: Changing fields make voltage
lessons.objective: Apply Faraday's law and the transformer rule.

concepts.title: Faraday's law
concepts.summary: The induced emf is the rate of change of flux times the number of turns: emf = N x (change in flux)/(change in time).

concepts.title: Transformer
concepts.summary: Voltage ratios follow turn ratios: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np.

misconceptions: A strong magnetic field induces a voltage. A changing flux does; a steady field of any size does not.
Lenz's law makes energy. The induced current opposes the change, which is why the effort of moving the magnet goes into the circuit.
Transformers work on direct current. They need a changing flux, so alternating current.
sequence: Move a magnet through a coil: a meter kicks when it moves and stays at zero when still.
Flux = B x A x cos(theta).
Faraday's law and the minus sign (Lenz).
Generators and the AC supply: spinning a coil.
Transformers and why power is sent at high voltage.
examples: 100 turns, area 0.010 m2, B going from 0 to 0.50 T in 0.20 s: flux change 0.0050 Wb, emf = 100 x 0.0050 / 0.20 = 2.5 V.
230 V across a 1000-turn primary with a 50-turn secondary gives 230 x 50/1000 = 11.5 V.

figures.shows: Flux against time with the emf as its slope, for three fixed cases.
Magnet moving through a coil with meter deflection, switchable.

questionPlan.sample: A coil has 100 turns. The flux through each turn changes by 0.0050 Wb in 0.20 s. What is the induced emf in volts?
A transformer has 1,000 primary turns and 50 secondary turns on a 230 V supply. What is the secondary voltage in volts?
A magnet rests inside a coil. What emf is induced?
questionPlan.answer: None, because the flux is not changing
choices: A large one, because the field is strong
None, because the flux is not changing

lessons.title: Light as an electromagnetic wave
lessons.objective: Connect changing fields to light and use the wave equation across the spectrum.

concepts.title: Electromagnetic wave
concepts.summary: Changing electric and magnetic fields sustain each other and travel at c = 3.00e8 m/s in a vacuum.

concepts.title: Spectrum
concepts.summary: Radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma are the same wave at different frequencies; c = f x wavelength.

misconceptions: Light needs a medium to travel through. Fields carry it; it crosses a vacuum.
Visible light is a separate thing from radio. They differ only in frequency.
Higher frequency light travels faster. In a vacuum all travel at c.
sequence: Faraday and Ampere-Maxwell in words: a changing B makes E and a changing E makes B.
That loop travels; Maxwell's speed from constants matches the measured speed of light (1865).
Lay out the spectrum by wavelength.
Use c = f lambda and time-of-flight.
Photon energy E = h f (introduce, do not develop).
examples: Light reaches us from the Moon in 3.844e8 m / 3.00e8 m/s = 1.28 s; from the Sun (1.496e11 m) in 499 s = 8.3 minutes.
A 2.45 GHz microwave oven wave has wavelength 3.00e8 / 2.45e9 = 0.122 m.

figures.shows: Spectrum bands with wavelength and frequency ranges.
figures.learnerAction: Select a band to see example uses.

figures.shows: Perpendicular E and B oscillations along the direction of travel.

questionPlan.sample: The Moon is 3.84e8 m away. Light travels at 3.00e8 m/s. How long does light take to arrive, in seconds to two decimals?
A microwave oven wave has frequency 2.45e9 Hz. What is its wavelength in metres to three decimals?
Which has the highest frequency?

historyNotes: James Clerk Maxwell showed in 1865 that his equations give a wave speed matching the measured speed of light and concluded that light is an electromagnetic wave. Heinrich Hertz produced radio waves in 1887 to 1888.

lessons.title: Heat and temperature
lessons.objective: Calculate heat transfer with specific and latent heats.

concepts.title: Specific heat
concepts.summary: Q = m c deltaT; water's c is 4,186 J/(kg K).

concepts.title: Latent heat
concepts.summary: Energy to change phase at a fixed temperature: fusion of ice 334 kJ/kg, vaporisation of water 2,260 kJ/kg.

misconceptions: Heat and temperature are the same. Heat is energy in transit; temperature measures how hot something is, and the same heat produces different rises in different masses.
Adding heat always raises temperature. During melting and boiling the temperature stays fixed while energy goes into changing phase.
Hot objects contain heat. They have internal energy; heat is only the transfer.
sequence: Temperature as average motion energy per particle; thermal equilibrium.
Q = m c deltaT with water, then metals.
The heating curve of ice to steam with its plateaus.
Calorimetry: energy lost by hot equals energy gained by cold.
Why water's high c keeps coasts mild (link to the Earth course).
examples: 2 kg of water heated 30 K: 2 x 4186 x 30 = 251,160 J.
1 kg at 80 degrees C mixed with 2 kg at 20 degrees C: final T = (80 + 40)/3 = 40 degrees C.

figures.shows: Heating curve for 1 kg ice from -20 degrees C: slopes and plateaus.

questionPlan.sample: How much energy heats 2 kg of water by 30 K? Use c = 4186 J/(kg K). Give the answer in joules.
1 kg of water at 80 degrees C is mixed with 2 kg of water at 20 degrees C. What is the final temperature in degrees C, ignoring losses?
How much energy melts 0.10 kg of ice at 0 degrees C? Use 334 kJ/kg, answer in kJ.

lessons.title: How heat moves
lessons.objective: Compute conduction rates and radiation power and see why insulation and colour matter.

concepts.title: Conduction
concepts.summary: Rate = k A deltaT / L through a layer of conductivity k, area A and thickness L.

concepts.title: Radiation
concepts.summary: A surface at temperature T (in kelvin) emits power epsilon sigma A T^4, with sigma = 5.67e-8 W/(m2 K4).

misconceptions: Thicker insulation lowers the temperature difference. It lowers the rate for the same difference; the rate falls as 1/L.
Cold flows into a warm room. Heat flows out of warm things; there is no flow of cold.
Only hot things radiate. Everything above absolute zero radiates; the rate goes with the fourth power of kelvin temperature.
sequence: Three routes: conduction, convection, radiation.
Conduction: rate set by material, area, difference and thickness.
Convection: moving fluid carries heat (link to the weather lesson).
Radiation: Stefan-Boltzmann; doubling temperature makes 16 times the power.
Apply to a window and to a thermos.
examples: A 2.0 m2 pane of glass 5.0 mm thick with k = 1.0 W/(m K) and 20 K difference conducts 1.0 x 2.0 x 20 / 0.005 = 8,000 W.
A black surface at 300 K emits 5.67e-8 x 300^4 = 459 W/m2; at 600 K it emits 16 times as much, 7,348 W/m2.

figures.shows: Wall cross-section with temperature profile through layers.
figures.learnerAction: Choose between one thick layer and two layers.

figures.shows: Radiated power against temperature on linear axes, showing the fourth-power rise.

lessons.title: Gases and the first law
lessons.objective: Use the ideal gas law and the first law of thermodynamics.

concepts.title: Ideal gas law
concepts.summary: PV = nRT with R = 8.314 J/(mol K) and T in kelvin.

concepts.title: First law
concepts.summary: The change in internal energy equals the heat added minus the work done by the gas: delta U = Q - W.

misconceptions: Temperature in the gas law can be in Celsius. It must be in kelvin.
Heat added always raises temperature. If the gas does work as it expands, energy leaves as work.
A gas has a smooth push on the walls. Pressure is the average of countless molecular collisions.
sequence: Molecular picture: pressure from collisions, temperature from average kinetic energy.
PV = nRT: three variables, one equation.
Work as pressure times change of volume, the area under a PV curve.
First law: energy conservation with heat and work.
Cases: isothermal, constant-volume, constant-pressure.
examples: A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work: delta U = 300 J.

figures.shows: PV diagram with an expansion path and the shaded area as work.
figures.learnerAction: Switch between isothermal and constant-pressure paths.

figures.shows: Piston and cylinder with molecules; temperature slider as fixed cases.

lessons.title: Engines and the limit
lessons.objective: Find the efficiency limit of a heat engine and compute entropy changes.

concepts.title: Carnot limit
concepts.summary: No engine between a hot reservoir at T_h and a cold one at T_c exceeds 1 - T_c/T_h (kelvin).

concepts.title: Entropy
concepts.summary: Heat Q entering at temperature T changes entropy by Q/T; the total never decreases in a real process.

misconceptions: A perfect engine could turn all heat into work. The second law forbids it; some must go to a colder place.
Efficiency depends on the engine's design alone. Even a perfect engine is limited by the two temperatures.
Entropy means disorder only. It is tied to how many ways energy can be spread, and to Q/T.
sequence: Why a car engine is not 100 percent efficient: heat in, work out, heat rejected.
Efficiency = W / Q_in.
Carnot's limit and why using a cooler exhaust helps.
Entropy as the bookkeeping for which processes run one way.
Heat pumps and refrigerators run the engine backwards.
examples: An engine takes 1,000 J, rejects 700 J: W = 300 J, efficiency 0.30.
Between 600 K and 300 K, the limit is 1 - 300/600 = 0.50. Melting 1 kg of ice at 273.15 K takes 334,000 J, so entropy rises by 334,000/273.15 = 1,223 J/K.

figures.shows: Engine diagram: hot reservoir, engine, work, cold reservoir with arrows sized by energy.
figures.learnerAction: Switch between real and Carnot cases.

figures.shows: Carnot efficiency against T_cold/T_hot.

questionPlan.sample: An engine takes in 1,000 J of heat and rejects 700 J. What is its efficiency as a decimal?
What is the Carnot efficiency between 700 K and 280 K, as a decimal?
Melting 1.0 kg of ice at 273.15 K absorbs 334,000 J. By how many J/K does the entropy of the ice rise, to the nearest J/K?

historyNotes: Sadi Carnot published his analysis of the limits of heat engines in 1824. Rudolf Clausius introduced the term entropy in 1865.
